media:group.media:title: 7 AI code review best practices #deeplearningai #qodo
media:group.media:description:
A pull request can look clean and still miss a requirement or hide a security issue. When AI writes more of your code, there is often too much to check by hand.
AI Code Review, built in collaboration with Qodo and taught by Nnenna Ndukwe, walks through 7 review practices with before and after examples. A few of them:
🔍Run the review before you open a pull request 🧑‍💻Use a reviewer that didn’t write the code 📂Give the reviewer task and repository context ⚖️Triage findings by risk 🔁Turn good feedback into reusable standards
💡The key lesson: the context you give your reviewer matters more than which model you use.
🛠️You’ll also build your own review agent. Start with a context engine (chunking, embeddings, vector search), then extend it into an ensemble of specialized reviewers.
📌Intermediate, about 1 hour, Python recommended.
👉Enroll now: https://www.deeplearning.ai/courses/ai-code-review

entry.title: Learn to build better AI Agents through better context

media:group.media:title: Learn to build better AI Agents through better context
media:group.media:description:
Learn More: https://bit.ly/4yy5iWP
The longer an agent works, the more repeated, contradictory, or stale information builds up in its context. Models perform worse as their context grows, a problem Jeff Huber and his team at Chroma named Context Rot.
In our new course, Context Engineering, taught by Jeff Huber alongside guest speaker Drew Breunig, you'll build agent harnesses from scratch in Python and learn to give agents the right information, in the right format, at the right time.
In this course, you'll learn: - Agentic search: Retrieve data with multiple search tools from different sources. Use traces to improve tool selection through evals. - Context management: Use pruning, compaction, and scratchpads to format the information an agent needs to complete a task. - Agentic memory: Store context from user feedback as reusable memories, retrieve it when a task needs it, and update records across sessions as information changes.
Enroll for free: https://bit.ly/4yy5iWP

entry.title: Build AI agents that learn from experience

media:group.media:title: Build AI agents that learn from experience
media:group.media:description:
Learn More: https://bit.ly/4iu7p9F
Introducing Building Adaptive AI Agents, a short course built in partnership with Oracle and taught by Nacho Martínez, Data Scientist Advocate at Oracle, and Casius Lee, AI Developer Advocate at Oracle.
Agents don't need to relearn the job every session: give them mechanisms to carry experience forward, and they get faster and more reliable with every run. Today's coding agents can write code, use tools, and carry out multi-step tasks, but each fresh session starts from zero. An agent that spent minutes fixing an environment issue yesterday will burn the same time and tokens rediscovering the fix today.
In this course, you'll work with three adaptation layers. For behavior adaptation, you'll build a skill induction pipeline that turns the agent's traces, its conversations, tool calls, errors, and fixes, into reusable skills it applies the next time it sees a similar task, with a human in the loop approving each skill. For knowledge adaptation, you'll build a code knowledge graph that connects files through imports, function calls, and co-edits in git history, so the agent retrieves context by navigating the structure of the codebase instead of relying on keyword search. For model adaptation, you'll learn when it makes sense to adapt the model itself with techniques like fine-tuning.
In detail, you'll:
Build a mental model for adaptive AI agents, including why forgetting is expensive and where an agent can improve. Build a skill induction pipeline that turns repeated experiences in an agent's traces into reusable skills the agent retrieves on similar tasks. See why retrieval, not code generation, is often the real bottleneck in large codebases, and where keyword and regex search miss the files that matter. Construct a code knowledge graph from imports, function calls, and co-edits in git history, then compare graph-based retrieval against regex matching and text search. Learn when and how weight-space adaptation, such as fine-tuning, can be the right tool.
By the end, you'll know how to build agents that get measurably better at the same work from one day to the next, instead of paying for the same mistakes twice.
Enroll Now: https://bit.ly/4iu7p9F
